Situation at a glance

            On 5 October 2026, WHO was informed about a laboratory-confirmed imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) in Kenya with travel history from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Kenya through Uganda. The patient was hospitalized and treated in Kenya but subsequently died on 5 October. Public health response measures have been initiated in Kenya and Uganda, including contact tracing. 

Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 25 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded to one additional health zone,  Alimbongo health zone in North Kivu, adding to the geographic footprint of an outbreak that remains concentrated in the eastern part of the country. 

As of 6 October 2026, the country has recorded 8728 confirmed cases and 4205 confirmed deaths, corresponding to a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.2%. The cases have been reported from 64 health zones across seven provinces out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo.  

At the national level, transmission remains intense, although the burden is unevenly distributed. In some areas, there are clear signs that the epidemic is slowing down, although in others it continues to grow. Over the past three completed epidemiological weeks, new weekly cases nationwide have increased by 2.5% from 475 to 487, while new weekly deaths remain stable at 224 compared to 222. 

The persistently high mortality, together with the large number of deaths occurring outside treatment centres, continues to point to delays in identifying illness and reaching appropriate care. Since the last Disease Outbreak News, 264 of the 372 reported deaths occurred in communities and 108 in treatment centres. 

On 1 October, the Netherlands reported the medical evacuation of a healthcare worker who tested positive by PCR for Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.  At the time of reporting, the patient has been undergoing treatment in the Netherlands. 

Description of the situation

Since the previous 
Disease Outbreak News

In the most recent 24-hour period, as of 6 October, 62 new confirmed cases were reported, with Ituri accounting for 33 cases and North Kivu for 30. No new cases were reported in Bas-Uélé, South Kivu or Sud-Ubangi during that period. Across the preceding seven days, the average number of new cases rose to 72 per day. 
As of 6 October, cumulative confirmed cases have reached 8728, including 4205 deaths and 2269 recoveries. The overall crude CFR is 48.2%.  
Confirmed cases have now been identified in 64 health zones across seven provinces. Forty-eight of the 64 affected zones reported at least one new case during the preceding 21 days, while 16 reported no recent cases. Ituri remains the most extensively affected province, with 28 of 36 health zones reporting cases during this outbreak, followed by North Kivu (17/34), Haut-Uélé (7/13), Tshopo (7/23), Bas-Uélé (3/11), South Kivu (1/34) and Sud-Ubangi (1/16). Alimbongo in North Kivu is the most recently affected health zone and reported four confirmed cases, including two deaths.

Ituri remains the epicentre, with 6480 cumulative confirmed cases and 2989 deaths. North Kivu follows with 1755 confirmed cases and 1013 deaths, and continues to record the highest provincial CFR, at 57.7%. Haut-Uélé has reported 364 cases and 153 deaths, while Tshopo has recorded 51 cases and 17 deaths. The less-affected provinces continue to report substantially fewer cases, but transmission persists in several of them. The most affected health zones were Beni and Katwa in North Kivu, and Rwampara, Bunia and Mandima in Ituri. The continued occurrence of cases across multiple provinces shows that the outbreak remains geographically active even as intensity varies between health zones. 
Contact follow-up remains a major operational pressure and has fluctuated below the response target in recent weeks. Coverage was 87.6% on 16 September, briefly above the target of 85%, but fell to 74.7% by 25 September. Although coverage subsequently improved to 82.0% on 27 September, it remained below target and stood at 80.4% in the latest reporting period, with 23 741 of 29 535 contacts reached as of 4 October. The current level therefore reflects a persistent gap in the ability to monitor exposed people consistently throughout the 21-day follow-up period.

Kenya  
On 6 October 2026, the Ministry of Health of Kenya reported the first laboratory-confirmed imported case of BVD in Kenya.  
According to an official statement from the Ministry of Health, the individual is an adult who lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient became ill approximately one month ago and was treated in several hospitals while in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The patient travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Kampala, Uganda, by road before arriving in Nairobi, Kenya by air on 3 October. It is currently unclear if and when he was symptomatic during these travels, but upon arriving ill in Kenya, the patient was transported by a relative directly to Nairobi Hospital and isolated in the facility. A sample collected from the patient on 5 October was positive for BDBV at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute Laboratory on the same day. The patient was given supportive treatment but subsequently died.  
A safe and dignified burial has been conducted. Public health response actions were immediately initiated. Contact tracing is ongoing, including for the international flight.  
Given the timelines of the illness, and the one month time from initial symptoms to death, it is presumed he was not initially sick with BVD, which does not usually have such a long progression from infection to symptoms and death, but became infected with BVD in a health facility or community while seeking care for another ailment.  
The Netherlands  
On 1 October 2026, the Netherlands reported the medical evacuation of a healthcare worker who tested positive by PCR for BDBV in the Democratic Republic of the Congo where the patient was working on the Ebola disease outbreak response. Following confirmation of the diagnosis, the patient was safely repatriated to the Netherlands under strict medical and infection-prevention procedures, in close coordination with the relevant health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Netherlands. As with previous medically evacuated cases, this case will not be reported as a local case of BVD in the Netherlands.

As of 20 October 2026, a total of 9704 confirmed cases, including 4687 deaths (crude case fatality ratio: 48.3%), have been reported across 66 health zones in eight provinces.  The high proportion of deaths occurring in communities continues to highlight challenges in early case detection and timely access to appropriate care. Of the 482 deaths reported since the previous update, 307 occurred in communities and 175 in treatment centres.

As of 20 October 2026, a total of nine cases of BVD including one death, has been reported in Kenya. The eight additional cases are all known contacts of the first imported case. There is currently no evidence of wider community transmission. 
On 20 October 2026, Nigeria confirmed an imported case in the Federal Capital Territory Abuja in a patient who had travelled from Uganda to the country. The patient is currently in isolation and receiving medical care. Further investigations are ongoing to better understand the complete travel history and the possible source of exposure. 
These developments underscore the need for sustained readiness in the region, including cross-border surveillance, points of entry monitoring, timely case detection and coordinated preparedness and response measures.

Strengthening community preparedness and resilience on health emergencies

Nairobi—
World Health Organization in the African Region has launched Resilience, Engagement, Acceleration for Community Health Across the African Region (REACH Africa), an initiative developed to strengthen community preparedness through institutionalized community engagement, innovative communication approaches and community-centred dialogue among communities, governments and partners.
Convened by WHO on 17 September 2026, the launch webinar brought together representatives from WHO country offices, ministries of health, community organizations, development partners and other stakeholders from across the African region. The webinar introduced REACH Africa, outlined its objectives and planned activities, and explored opportunities for collaboration and engagement. Supporting implementation of the WHO African Region’s Community Protection and Resilience Strategy for Community Engagement (2023–2030), REACH Africa translates regional commitments into practical action to strengthen community preparedness and resilience across the region’s 47 Member States.
The initiative recognizes communities as essential partners in preventing, preparing for, responding to and recovering from public health emergencies. Lessons from Ebola, COVID-19, cholera, mpox and other health emergencies have demonstrated that meaningful and sustained community engagement is critical to building trust, strengthening preparedness and ensuring effective emergency response.
"Communities are essential for building trust, identifying hotspots, understanding household-level
Dynamics and detecting early signals," said Dr Dick Chamla, Programme Area Manager and Coordinator at the WHO Regional Emergency Preparedness and Response Hub in Nairobi, Kenya. "REACH Africa will help turn this approach into practical action across the continent, connecting communities, health systems and partners to build stronger, more resilient health security."
REACH Africa provides a regional platform for collaboration, knowledge exchange and shared learning to support Member States in strengthening community-centred preparedness. The initiative will leverage the REACH Africa podcast series and “community dialogues on wheels” (EngageMobile) under the REACHConnect platforms to strengthen community preparedness and resilience. The podcast series will demystify preparedness concepts, share practical, community-led approaches and promote cross-country learning, while EngageMobile will facilitate two-way dialogue between communities, health workers, decision-makers, WHO and partners, ensuring that community perspectives inform preparedness, response and health system strengthening.
Through these platforms, REACH Africa will strengthen collaboration between communities and health authorities, facilitate learning across countries and promote evidence-informed approaches to community engagement and preparedness. The initiative will provide opportunities for WHO country offices, ministries of health, development partners, civil society organizations and communities to exchange experiences, showcase innovations and work together to strengthen preparedness and resilience.
“This initiative will give us a shared platform to listen to communities, address their concerns and turn their priorities into action. We are excited to see this initiative grow at the grassroots level and put communities at the heart of preparedness and resilience,” said Dr Desta Negesso Abunko, a public health specialist from Ethiopia.
As countries continue to strengthen their capacity to prevent, prepare for and respond to health emergencies, REACH Africa will help amplify community voices, share successful practices and advance sustainable, people-centred approaches to health security across the African Region.
“Preparedness starts with communities,” said Dr Julienne Anoko, Risk Communication and Community Engagement Officer at WHO’s Nairobi hub. “Together, we can build stronger communities, stronger health systems and a more resilient Africa”.

Kenya readies its military medical team to protect communities ahead of El Niño rains

More pictures

More images

Nairobi-
 With El Niño rains forecast for October to December 2026, the Kenya Defence Forces is strengthening its emergency medical capacity to support national response efforts when local health services come under pressure.
Floods do more than damage homes. They block access to clinics, contaminate water, and push families into crowded camps where diseases such as cholera spread quickly. Kenya has already seen the cost this year. Flooding during the March to May long rains affected 27 counties, triggered landslides in Tharaka-Nithi, Elgeyo-Marakwet and Kiambu, and cut communities off from essential services. In May 122 deaths and more than 42,000 people were affected.
The Kenya Meteorological Department forecasts El Niño conditions and above-average rainfall across much of the country. A national assessment has identified 18 counties and 5,660 health facilities in at-risk areas, and rates overall flood preparedness at 54 per cent. Key structures are in place, but serious gaps remain.
Kenya is acting on several fronts. An El Niño Contingency Plan is in place, the Ministry of Health and the National Disaster Operations Centre have activated joint planning meetings, and counties are being supported to assess their own preparedness.
The Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) has been building an emergency medical team for this kind of crisis, a trained group that deploys during disasters to treat the sick and injured and keep essential care running. Thirty KDF health professionals completed induction training in 2024, and the team now has a leadership structure and written procedures.
Strengthening the team's foundations 
From 8 to 11 September 2026, the Kenya Defence Force health security team and WHO experts took that work further. They formed a core management team with clear leadership roles, developed standard operating procedures for clinical care, logistics, and water, sanitation and hygiene, and trained its first 30 team members.
Participants also reviewed the roadmap towards establishing a WHO-accredited Type 1 fixed Emergency Medical Team, which would provide medical care to large numbers of patients from a fixed location during emergencies. Once established, the team would serve as a national resource for large-scale emergency response.
Testing the response before the floods arrive
With these foundations in place, participants also conducted a tabletop exercise to identify potential gaps early. They worked through a scenario in which heavy rains caused flooding, forcing families from their homes, followed by a cholera outbreak in displacement camps.
At each stage, they discussed how the team would activate, coordinate with national and county health authorities, mobilise resources, deliver clinical, public health and sanitation services, and finally hand over and withdraw. The exercise exposed procedures that need amending and clarified who coordinates with whom, inside and outside KDF. 
"As KDF, it is expected of us to be called upon when our time comes. If the systems are overwhelmed, we can be an important national asset. We are not working alone. We are part of a team," said Director of Medical Services, Major General (Dr) Francis Kuria, the Chief of Clinical Support Services. 
Participants closed the week by developing an El Niño preparedness and response plan. This sets out the scenarios Kenya could face and the priority actions the team would take to respond to flooding and the health emergencies that follow. 
Working as one system
Emergencies of this scale demand a whole of government response. The exercise clarified how the team would work with the Ministry of Health, county authorities and other agencies.
"Preparedness is about testing systems before they are needed. Exercises like this help us work through scenarios and address gaps before an emergency occurs. WHO will continue working with KDF and its partners ahead of the El Niño season and beyond," said Dr Martins Livinus, Team Lead for Emergency Preparedness and Response, WHO Kenya.

Kenya confirms first imported Bundibugyo virus disease case; WHO supports control efforts

Nairobi—
Following the confirmation by Kenyan authorities of the country's first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Government of Kenya to intensify key control measures to prevent further spread of the virus.
The government is strengthening its response coordination and case investigation, while monitoring and listing contacts for enhanced disease surveillance. At the core of the response efforts are screening at high-risk points of entry, and clear risk communication, while engaging communities to help prevent infection. These measures are rapidly being deployed to ensure the identification of cases and help contain further transmission.
The patient, a Kenyan citizen, fell ill in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where they had been living, and was treated at several health facilities there. The patient then travelled by road to Kampala, Uganda through Beni on 2 October 2026, and flew to Nairobi, arriving on 3 October 2026. On arrival, the patient was transported to a hospital in Nairobi and was quickly isolated. Samples tested positive for Bundibugyo virus at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute. Despite supportive care, the patient died on the night of 5 October 2026 and was buried on 6 October 2026 in line with the country’s Ebola safe and dignified burial protocol.
The Government of Kenya notified WHO of the case in line with the International Health Regulations (2005) on 6 October 2026. Kenya is the fourth country to confirm BVD. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is responding to an ongoing BVD outbreak, while Uganda, where the Bundibugyo virus species was first detected in 2007, ended the latest outbreak in August 2026. Most cases in Uganda were imported from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the remaining few were locally acquired among contacts and health workers linked to imported cases. France reported a travel-related case of BVD in June 2026.
Health authorities in Kenya have so far listed 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient. They are also tracing 23 passengers and four crew members from the same flight, with arrangements underway for appropriate follow-up and quarantine of people assessed to be at risk.
"Health emergency preparedness gives us a head start. Kenya has put important outbreak control measures in place. The priority now is to move swiftly to detect any further cases before the virus has an opportunity to spread. We're supporting the ongoing efforts to strengthen the response, and with rapid and coordinated action, we can prevent the virus from gaining a foothold and stop a potential larger outbreak," said Dr Mohamed Janabi, WHO Regional Director for Africa.
Kenya has been on high alert since May 2026, when outbreaks were declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. As of 6 October 2026, Kenya has screened over 652 000 travellers entering the country, tested 267 suspected samples and trained around 5000 health workers on Ebola prevention and management.
WHO and partners have supported Kenya’s Ministry of Health and National Public Health Institute in these efforts. This includes Ebola simulation exercises and training a national pool of rapid response trainers, among them responders who served during the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak. Isolation units across 27 high-risk counties in Kenya have been identified and assessed, case managers trained, and Ebola surveillance tools have been updated so that suspected cases can be quickly identified, reported and investigated. Risk communication and community engagement activities have also been strengthened through public messaging, media and community engagement, call centre support, and monitoring and responding to rumours and misinformation.
WHO has also delivered about 1000 Ebola tests and 1000 personal protective equipment kits to high-risk counties in Kenya.
Kenya's Ebola preparedness score, which tracks progress on key readiness measures such as surveillance, laboratory testing, isolation and treatment facilities and trained response teams, rose from 66% in May to 82% in July 2026.
WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or Kenya based on the currently available information. WHO continues to closely monitor and, where necessary, verify travel and trade measures in relation to this event.
WHO calls for continued support to the response in affected countries. Global solidarity, along with government-led responses with engaged communities, is the best route to ending the outbreak.
Note to editors:
Bundibugyo virus disease is a severe, often fatal illness. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. There are currently no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo virus disease, but candidate products are being evaluated in clinical trials.

Nairobi -
 To support the Ministry of Health’s response to Kenya’s first confirmed imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease, the World Health Organization (WHO) has this week handed over essential medical supplies worth around US$70 000 to help protect frontline health workers and speed up the testing of suspected cases.
“Those who face the greatest risk are the men and women on the front line, our nurses, doctors, clinical officers, laboratory staff, public health officers and community health promoters,” 
said Mary Muthoni, Principal Secretary for Public Health and Professional Standards in remarks delivered on behalf of Hon. Aden Duale, Cabinet Secretary for Health. 
“They walk towards the danger so that the rest of us may be safe, and we owe them nothing less than full protection. No health worker in this country should be asked to attend to a suspected Ebola case without the right protective equipment.”
The supplies include personal protective equipment such as hazmat suits, isolation gowns, goggles and face shields, as well as Ebola testing kits and biohazard containers for the safe transport of samples to the laboratory, infrared thermometers for screening, and disinfectant sprayers, waste bags and sharps safety boxes for infection prevention and control. The Ministry of Health will distribute them to the facilities and teams where they are needed most. 
“Protecting health workers is essential to saving lives,” 
said Dr Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo, WHO Representative to Kenya. 
“This donation will help reduce the risk of infection in health facilities, support safe patient management and ensure continuity of essential services. We hope these supplies will give confidence to health workers, knowing that supplies are there to protect them in the event that any patient comes up with the disease.”
The supplies were mobilized through the WHO Regional Emergency Preparedness and Response Hub in Nairobi. 
“Kenya has kindly hosted the regional emergency preparedness and response hub, and therefore we are able to get supplies readily at short notice,”
 said Dr Kimambo. 
“The hub has also facilitated rapid deployment of supplies to other countries in the region when needed.”
The Ministry of Health and the Kenya National Public Health Institute are leading the national response. Since the case was confirmed, they have listed 127 contacts, 94 of whom are in quarantine, and screened over 665 000 travellers at points of entry. Five laboratories have been designated to test for the disease, including two mobile laboratories at the Busia and Bungoma borders, and nearly 5000 health workers have been trained.  
“I commend the Kenyan government for its prompt action and for reporting the case to WHO under the International Health Regulations in a timely way,”
 said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus at a media briefing on 7 October.
“WHO continues to work with the Ministry of Health and the Kenya National Public Health Institute to strengthen the response through simulation exercises, training of rapid response teams, surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory coordination, case management, and infection prevention and control,”
 said Dr Kimambo. 
“Equally important is risk communication and community engagement. We will continue to support the Ministry to provide timely, accurate information, address misinformation and strengthen community trust, which is critical at this time.”
Kenya is the fourth country to confirm Bundibugyo virus disease. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has an ongoing outbreak, with over 8700 confirmed cases, and Uganda ended its outbreak in August 2026. France and Kenya have each recorded one imported case. WHO advises against travel or trade restrictions on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or Kenya.

Setting Kenya’s research agenda on health, migration and displacement

Nairobi
—
The
 Ministry of Health, Kenya, WHO's Health and Migration Programme and the WHO Kenya Country Office, jointly convened a technical consultation to support the development of Kenya's National Research Agenda on Health, Migration and Displacement.
The consultation brought together thirty-two representatives from government, United Nations agencies, academic and research institutions, civil society organizations and partner organizations to validate and prioritize evidence gaps and develop a roadmap and action plan for strengthening research on health, migration and displacement in Kenya.
"Health operates on facts and figures. Migrants and refugees have a lot of health needs, and most of the time they are forgotten. Some are pregnant women, some are old people, some are children under five who need to be vaccinated. We must address the health issues not only of refugees but also of host communities," said John Ndungu, Director of Public Health, Ministry of Health, Kenya.
As migration and displacement continue to shape health needs and service delivery globally and nationally, robust evidence is essential to inform policy, planning and programme implementation. Mobility can affect access to services, continuity of care and wider determinants of health, making it essential that health systems are equipped to respond effectively to the needs of migrant and displaced populations while also strengthening health outcomes for host communities.
Evidence can support more inclusive, responsive and resilient health systems, improving health outcomes for all.
"If we co-create these policies and involve the people who are concerned, those policies will be people-centred. Their uptake may be higher because they are relevant and appropriate to the communities," said Professor Salome Bukachi, Chair, Department of Anthropology, Gender and African Studies, University of Nairobi. 
Building on findings from a scoping review and pre-consultation engagements, participants determined priority evidence gaps across a range of thematic areas and explored opportunities to strengthen collaboration between researchers, policymakers, practitioners and communities.
Discussions highlighted the importance of ensuring that future research responds to national and subnational priorities and contributes to evidence-informed policy and decision-making.
The consultation represents an important step in operationalizing and contextualizing the WHO global research agenda on health, migration and displacement,  adapted to Kenya's context to identify evidence needs that can support national action.

Participants emphasized the need to strengthen the generation, use and translation of evidence, including through implementation research, improved knowledge-sharing, and stronger collaboration across sectors. Discussions also highlighted the importance of meaningful engagement with migrant and displaced populations and the organizations that work alongside them, recognizing the value of lived experience in shaping both research priorities and processes to translate research into policy and action.

"This agenda belongs to Kenya, and that is its strength. WHO will continue to support the Ministry of Health and partners to turn these priorities into action at national and county levels, so that migrants, refugees, displaced populations as well as host communities are not left behind on Kenya's path to universal health coverage," said Dr Neema Kimambo, WHO Representative to Kenya.

Feature Story

Ebola response: Disinformation kills, care saves lives

WHO supports Kenya’s Ebola response as third case is found early in quarantine 

Nairobi - 
The World Health Organization (WHO) is supporting the Ministry of Health’s response after Kenya confirmed its second and third cases of Bundibugyo Ebola, on 14 and 16 October. The two patients, a 39-year-old man and a 65-year-old woman, are both close family members of Kenya’s first case and were already in quarantine when they fell ill. Kenya has now confirmed three cases, including one death.
Kenya’s first case, a Kenyan man who had travelled home from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, died on the night of 5 October. It was the first Ebola case ever recorded in Kenya. Health teams quickly identified 130 people who had been in contact with him, including family members, friends, health workers who cared for him and people who travelled on the same flight.
By 16 October, 127 of the 130 contacts listed by the Ministry were in quarantine, with daily temperature and symptom checks for 21 days, the longest it can take for someone to fall ill after exposure.
“Being quarantined means the family and the general public are better protected from exposure to the virus, hence reducing chances of community transmission,” says Dr Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo, WHO Representative to Kenya.
Ebola is not spread through the air. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of a person who is sick with, or has died from, the disease, or with objects contaminated by these fluids.
The early signs of Bundibugyo Ebola look like malaria and other common illnesses, and include fever, tiredness, muscle or joint pains, headache and sore throat. Later signs can include vomiting, diarrhoea and impaired kidney and liver functions. Many people believe that bleeding is a common sign of Ebola. In fact, it is less common, and when it happens it usually appears later in the illness.
There is no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo Ebola yet, although trials are under way in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Both patients are receiving supportive care, such as fluids to prevent dehydration and treatment of their symptoms, in designated treatment units. Early supportive care improves the chance of survival. The Ministry of Health reports that the second patient is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.
People with Ebola cannot pass it on before they have symptoms, so isolating both patients at their very first symptoms keep the chance of them passing the virus to others low.
“This is the response working as designed,” said Dr Patrick Amoth, Director General for Health, Ministry of Health.
Both new cases are linked to the first, imported case, and the Ministry of Health has confirmed that “there is no evidence of community transmission of the disease”. The Ministry has also noted that further cases among quarantined contacts are possible until their monitoring ends, and that any such cases will be detected and treated just as quickly.
Kenya began preparing for a possible Ebola case in May 2026, when the outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and nearly 5000 health workers have since been trained, with support from WHO, to recognize the disease and care for patients safely. Since the first case was confirmed, WHO has been supporting the Ministry of Health across the response, from coordination, surveillance and contact tracing to laboratory testing, patient care, infection prevention and control, health checks at points of entry, and risk communication and community engagement. WHO has also handed over supplies worth around US$ 70 000, including protective equipment, Ebola testing kits and infrared thermometers for screening travellers.
WHO advises against closing borders or restricting trade. The Ministry of Health has confirmed that Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
“The two new cases have been detected early because they were already in quarantine and were being checked every day,” said Dr Kimambo. “WHO commends the Ministry of Health, the Kenya National Public Health Institute and the national and county health teams for their swift action. We thank the health workers, response teams and families in quarantine for their commitment.”
As the remaining contacts complete their 21 days of monitoring, contact tracing and quarantine will continue to be Kenya’s first line of defence. Each daily check is a chance to find illness early, give patients the best chance of recovery, and help keep the virus out of the wider community. WHO will continue to support the Ministry of Health and County Health Teams in this work.

Nairobi
—Today 20 contacts associated with Kenya’s first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease were released from quarantine and reunited with their families after completing the mandatory 21-day monitoring period.

All eight cases were already in quarantine at the time and were immediately transferred to the country’s Ebola treatment centre in Nairobi. Summary

DRC

WHO
 Director-General determined that the outbreak constitutes 
a public health emergency of international concern.

DRC

WHO
 Emergency Committee meeting

25 October 2026
, 10,060 confirmed cases and 4,887 confirmed deaths have been reported in the 
DRC
. This is an increase of 508 confirmed cases and 285 deaths since the last 
Outbreaks Under Monitoring
 report. Cases have been reported in 66 health zones across 8 provinces (Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, South-Ubangi, North-Ubangi, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele and Tshopo). The highest number of cases have been reported in Ituri (7,211 cases, including 3,370 deaths), followed by North Kivu (2,309 cases, including 1,293 deaths) and Haut-Uele (436 cases, including 190 deaths) provinces. The heterogeneous transmission patterns across the provinces have resulted in a high and fluctuating incidence pattern nationally. Between 6 and 20 October 2026, 
482 new deaths
 were reported, of which 307 deaths occurred in the community and 175 deaths were in treatment centres. The high proportion of community deaths emphasises the challenges in early case detection and timely access to appropriate care. This has become the largest recorded 
BVD
 outbreak and is the second largest Ebola disease outbreak to date.

6 October 2026
, Kenya’s Ministry of Health reported the first confirmed case of 
BVD
 in Kenya, imported from the 
DRC
. The case travelled from the 
DRC
 to Kampala, Uganda, by road and arrived in Nairobi via a flight on 3 October 2026. Samples from the case tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus. The case was given supportive treatment but died on 5 October 2026. As of 26 October 2026, a total of

BVD

Summary

On 30 September 2026, 
Brazil reported
 a confirmed human case of swine influenza A(H1N1)v infection in an adult woman with pre-existing chronic conditions in Santa Catarina. The case experienced the onset of influenza-like illness on 16 July 2026 and sought medical care on 20 July 2026. The case was hospitalised on 27 July and received treatment, including oseltamivir, and intensive care including ventilatory support. The individual later died on 28 August 2026.

 Members of the case’s household, 4 adult individuals, also experienced influenza-like illness. They were diagnosed with a viral infection based on clinical examination and received treatment. Epidemiological investigations found that the case had no travel history or direct contact with swine, however, may have had indirect exposure to swine through a neighbour who raises swine for personal consumption. 
 The public health risk from current known influenza A viruses detected at the human-animal interface is 
assessed as low

WHO
. Sustained human-to-human transmission of these viruses is currently considered unlikely.
